Today you start drafting, and you will craft your sentences so readers can picture and understand your ideas."},{"type":"paragraph","audience":"shared","text":"Display two versions of one idea. Version A: Percy is brave. Version B: Gripping his pen-sword, Percy, a nervous twelve-year-old, steps toward the monster. Do the same with a film shot: a camera looking up at a character from a low angle."},{"type":"directions","text":"Turn to a partner. Compare the two versions. Which one gives you a stronger impression, and what makes it stronger?"},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"Which version creates a stronger picture, and why?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"Version B, because it has details like gripping the pen-sword and nervous, so I can see Percy. It's like a close-up in a movie that makes you feel his fear. Version A just tells me."},{"type":"teacher-note","variant":"tip","text":"Keep this to about two minutes of partner talk. Point out that visual language, like camera angle or lighting in film, and descriptive words in writing both shape the impression an audience gets."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"say","text":"Today you will learn to use sentence patterns, not just details, to guide how readers feel and understand your writing."}]}]},{"kind":"literacy-lab","title":"Literacy Lab","purpose":"Teach sentence expansion and varied openings through sentence combining, using the model essay, so students can craft analytical commentary.","activities":[{"id":"lab-sentence-expansion","title":"Sentence Combining: Expand and Vary","minutes":10,"standards":["L.6.3","L.6.3.a","W.6.2.d"],"routine":"Sentence Combining","blocks":[{"type":"paragraph","audience":"shared","text":"Display these short evidence sentences: Persephone eats pomegranate seeds. She must stay in the underworld. The seasons change. Display also: Maui steals fire. Maui is a trickster. He helps people."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"teach","text":"Three short sentences in a row sound choppy. We can expand and combine them. An appositive renames a noun: Persephone, the daughter of Demeter, eats pomegranate seeds. A prepositional phrase adds where or when: In the underworld, ... A subordinating clause shows a relationship: Because she eats the seeds, she must stay."},{"type":"paragraph","audience":"shared","text":"Model: Because Persephone, the daughter of Demeter, eats pomegranate seeds, she must return to the underworld each year, which explains why the seasons change."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"Which parts expand the sentence, and how does the opening differ from Persephone eats?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"The appositive 'the daughter of Demeter' adds who she is. The clause 'which explains why the seasons change' connects the myth to the world. It starts with Because instead of the name, so it sounds different from the other sentences."},{"type":"directions","text":"Combine the Maui sentences into one or two sentences. Use at least one appositive and start with something other than Maui. Share with a partner."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"What opening did you choose, and what does it emphasize?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"I wrote, 'Although Maui, a clever trickster, steals fire, he does it to help people.' Starting with Although shows the surprising contrast."},{"type":"teacher-note","variant":"note","text":"Watch for run-ons from over-combining. Limit combined sentences to one main idea. Have students read aloud to hear the flow."},{"type":"eld-panel","purpose":"Students expand noun phrases and combine sentences to add detail and precision.","sayAsk":"Say: 'Let's add details to the noun.' Ask: 'Who is Maui? What can we add?' Frames: ___, a ___, ___ (verb). Because ___, ___. In the ___, ___.","watchFor":"If students only add adjectives, then model an appositive with commas. If students lose the verb in a long sentence, then have them underline the subject and verb. Success: student writes one expanded sentence with an appositive or clause."},{"type":"support-table","rows":[{"situation":"Struggling with: Combining sentences without run-ons","tryThis":"Provide a frame such as 'Because ___, ___, ___.' and have students read it aloud, checking for one subject and verb in each part."},{"situation":"Ready for extension","tryThis":"Have students write the same idea with three different openings and choose which best fits their essay's focus."}]}]}]},{"kind":"learning-in-action","title":"Learning in Action","purpose":"Model craft with an example essay, then students draft an introduction and body paragraph with evidence and analysis, and exchange peer feedback.","activities":[{"id":"lia-model-craft","title":"Model: Craft in an Example Essay","minutes":8,"standards":["L.6.3","L.6.3.a","W.6.2.b","W.6.2.c","W.6.2.d","MSLS.6.2.2.a"],"routine":"Annotation","blocks":[{"type":"text-reference","title":"Model explanatory essay on myths across cultures","pages":"Introduction and first body paragraph"},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"say","text":"I will read the introduction and first body paragraph. Notice how the writer hooks you, names the myths, states the idea, and then connects evidence to analysis."},{"type":"directions","text":"Annotate as you listen. Underline varied sentence openings. Circle precise academic verbs such as reveals, illustrates and suggests. Box transitions."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"teach","text":"Strong introductions have a hook, brief context about the myths, and a thesis. Body paragraphs use a pattern: claim, evidence, analysis. Transitions like similarly, in contrast and as a result show how ideas connect."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"How does the writer vary sentences, and what impression does the visual language create?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"The writer starts one sentence with a clause, another with a phrase, and another with the subject, so it doesn't sound repetitive. Words like 'scorched earth' help me picture the myth, like a dramatic camera angle."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"How does the writer move from evidence to analysis?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"After the quote, the writer uses 'This reveals that...' to explain what the evidence means about values."},{"type":"pulse-check","standards":["W.6.2.b","L.6.3.a"],"stem":"In the model paragraph, why does the writer follow a detail from the myth with a sentence beginning 'This reveals that...'?","choices":[{"text":"To explain what the evidence shows about the myth's lesson or value","correct":true,"rationale":"Analysis sentences connect evidence to the essay's idea."},{"text":"To retell more of the myth's plot","correct":false,"rationale":"Students may think more plot equals more support, but the phrase signals explanation, not retelling."},{"type":"x","text":"To make the paragraph longer","correct":false,"rationale":"Length is not the purpose; the sentence adds meaning."},{"text":"To introduce a new myth","correct":false,"rationale":"The phrase continues the current idea instead of changing topics."}]},{"type":"eld-panel","purpose":"Students read closely and notice how sentence structures and noun phrases build meaning.","sayAsk":"Say: 'Find a sentence with a long noun phrase.' The evidence shows ___.","watchFor":"If students retell the myth, then prompt: 'What does the evidence show about values?' If students cannot find openings, then number the sentences and have them circle the first word. Include a hook, the names of your myths and their cultures, and a thesis statement. Use at least one appositive or subordinating clause, and vary your sentence openings."},{"type":"paragraph","audience":"shared","text":"Thesis frames: Although ___ and ___ come from different cultures, both myths teach that ___. If a thesis only names the myths, ask 'What do they teach?' Students may type if the class has technology (W.6.6)."},{"type":"eld-panel","purpose":"Students write a formal introduction with expanded noun phrases and precise vocabulary.","sayAsk":"Say: 'Tell your partner your thesis first.' The myth of ___ explains ___.","watchFor":"If students write only a topic sentence, then add because or although. If students use informal words, then swap for precise terms like reveals or illustrates. Success: student writes a thesis with a hook and context."},{"type":"support-table","rows":[{"situation":"Struggling with: Writing a thesis","tryThis":"Give a fill-in thesis frame and have students say the idea aloud before writing."},{"situation":"Ready for extension","tryThis":"Add a hook using vivid, visual language that creates an impression of the myth's world."}]}]},{"id":"lia-draft-body","title":"Draft a Body Paragraph","minutes":8,"standards":["W.6.2.b","W.6.2.c","W.6.2.d","W.6.9","L.6.3.a"],"routine":"Independent Writing","blocks":[{"type":"directions","text":"Draft one body paragraph. Use claim, evidence from a myth, and analysis. Use a transition, a precise academic verb, and at least two different sentence openings."},{"type":"paragraph","audience":"shared","text":"Analysis starters: This reveals that ___. The detail of ___ illustrates ___. As a result, ___. In contrast, ___."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"What evidence did you choose, and what does it show?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"I chose the part where Persephone eats the seeds. It illustrates that choices have consequences, which is a value in the myth."},{"type":"eld-panel","purpose":"Students develop a paragraph by linking evidence to analysis with transitions.","sayAsk":"Say: 'First give the evidence, then explain.' Ask: 'What does this detail show?' Frames: In the myth, ___. This shows ___. As a result, ___.","watchFor":"If students retell, then prompt for an analysis starter. If students string short sentences, then combine with an appositive. Success: paragraph has evidence and analysis."},{"type":"support-table","rows":[{"situation":"Struggling with: Connecting evidence to analysis","tryThis":"Provide a three-part frame: Claim, 'In the myth, ___,' 'This reveals ___.'"},{"situation":"Ready for extension","tryThis":"Add a comparison transition linking the second myth to the first in the same paragraph."}]}]},{"id":"lia-peer-feedback","title":"Peer Feedback on Clarity and Cohesion","minutes":4,"standards":["W.6.2.c","W.6.4","L.6.3.a"],"routine":"Partner Feedback","blocks":[{"type":"directions","text":"Swap drafts. Check for one expanded sentence, varied openings and transitions."},{"type":"paragraph","audience":"shared","text":"Feedback frames: One strength is ___. I could follow your idea when ___. You could connect ___ by adding a transition such as ___."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"What feedback will you use to improve your draft?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"My partner said my sentences all start with the myth's name. I will start one with Because to vary it and add a transition."},{"type":"teacher-note","variant":"note","text":"Keep feedback specific and kind. Listen for comments that point to words in the draft."}]}]},{"kind":"look-back","title":"Look Back","purpose":"Students reflect on their sentence craft and set a next step for the draft.","activities":[{"id":"look-back-quick-write","title":"Quick Write: Craft Reflection","minutes":5,"standards":["L.6.3.a","W.6.10"],"routine":"Quick Write","blocks":[{"type":"directions","text":"Write a few sentences in response to the question."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"Which sentence in your draft shows your best craft, and what is your next step?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"My best sentence is the one with the appositive, because it adds detail about Persephone without a new sentence. My next step is to finish my second body paragraph and add transitions."},{"type":"paragraph","audience":"shared","text":"Optional starter: My strongest sentence is ___ because ___.
